bull_thesis: KBR is a sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately) story trading at a conglomerate discount right before management splits it in two. The stock is $35.71 on the New York Stock Exchange, down about 45% over the past year and sitting near its 52-week low of $29.94 — the market is treating the whole company as one low-quality government contractor. It is really two very different businesses. Sustainable Technology Solutions (STS) is a capital-light, technology-led engineering and licensing arm — proprietary ammonia, sustainable-aviation-fuel (PureSAF) and plastics-recycling technology, plus high-return joint ventures (Brown & Root, the Plaquemines LNG project) — running 'twenty-plus percent' EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization) margins on roughly $2.2B of revenue, with a growing backlog and an energy-security tailwind. Mission Technology Solutions (MTS) is the larger, roughly $5.3B government, defense, space and intelligence services arm — lower margin near 9-10% but carrying a record $19.1B of backlog and options (up 15% year over year), $17B of bids awaiting award, and recent marquee wins including an $8B, 20-year National Science Foundation Antarctic support contract and a $2.5B NASA human-spaceflight recompete. Management has approved a spin-off that lists MTS as its own company, targeted for the second half of 2026, and has already named that company's chief executive and chief financial officer (June 2026) — a firm, scheduled event. Valuing each segment on its own peer multiple and subtracting about $2.49B of net debt gets to roughly $47 per share in the base case, well above both today's price and the Street's roughly $36 target. Insiders agree: four open-market buys against one sale, and a new roughly $24M stake disclosed in May. Management delivers on what it controls — margins expanded about 100 basis points in 2025, operating-cash conversion ran 110-130%, and the company has beaten earnings every quarter. The case depends on STS earning its premium multiple once standalone, MTS's roughly $3B of protested awards beginning to convert, and the spin completing on schedule.
bear_thesis: The discount may be deserved, and the break-up is not free money. Revenue is barely growing (+0.6% year over year) and MTS revenue actually fell 5% in the first quarter of 2026 as European contingency work ran off. The government side is dogged by award delays, a protest backlog, shutdown-disrupted contracting offices and NASA softness that management keeps promising will 'convert next year' — a refrain now more than a year old. Government-technology services multiples have compressed across the sector on budget-efficiency fears, so MTS may spin at a low multiple rather than unlock value. Leverage is real: net debt of about $2.49B is roughly 2.9x EBITDA, and management has said both companies must carry 'appropriate capital structures from day one,' meaning the new spin-off will be loaded with debt that eats into the per-share upside. Management's credibility took a hit when U.S. TRANSCOM abruptly terminated the HomeSafe military-moving contract in mid-2025, one quarter after leadership called the relationship 'strong' and said it was 'very confident in the future of this program' — a reminder that the biggest government programs can vanish overnight. The discounted-cash-flow and earnings-power-value models both show deeply negative margin of safety, reflecting lumpy, low-return, project-based cash flows. If STS fails to re-rate and MTS spins into a weak government-services tape, the parts are worth closer to $32 — below today's price. What confirms the bear: a soft second-quarter print on July 30, a spin delay, or the spin-off taking on heavy debt.
sop_breakdown: Segment sum-of-the-parts. Sustainable Technology Solutions: about $2.2B revenue at roughly a 20% EBITDA margin is about $435M, valued at about 11x (a premium for proprietary technology, capital-light economics and high-return joint-venture earnings) is roughly $4.8B of enterprise value. Mission Technology Solutions: about $5.3B revenue at roughly 9.5% EBITDA is about $510M, valued at about 8.75x (in line with de-rated government-services peers) is roughly $4.5B. Subtract about $0.35B for capitalized corporate overhead to reach about $8.9B of enterprise value; subtract about $2.49B of net debt to reach about $6.4B of equity; divide by roughly 127M shares for about $50, haircut to about $47 base case for spin-timing, leverage and execution risk. Adverse case (STS about 9x, MTS about 7x) is about $32; favorable case (STS about 13x, MTS about 10x) is about $66. Note the screener's own segment-percentage line understated MTS — MTS is the larger revenue segment, STS the smaller high-margin one (confirmed against the fiscal-2024 clean split of Government Solutions $5.87B versus STS $1.87B).
risk_reward: At $35.71, the adverse sum-of-the-parts sits near $32 (about a tenth below today, roughly the 52-week-low zone), while the base case near $47 is about a third higher and the favorable case near $66 is well above. Downside is cushioned by a deeply washed-out price, active insider buying and a hard, scheduled break-up catalyst; upside depends on the high-margin STS business earning a premium multiple once standalone and on MTS's record backlog converting. The skew is favorable, but a second-quarter earnings print about three weeks out and elevated leverage argue for a disciplined entry rather than chasing.
peer_comps_note: Closest public comparables are Jacobs (J, about $126) and Fluor (FLR, about $51) in diversified engineering and government services, with AECOM (ACM, about $68), Tetra Tech (TTEK, about $31) and MasTec (MTZ, about $375) as adjacents. KBR trades at roughly 7.5x enterprise value to EBITDA on a blended basis — a clear discount to higher-quality Jacobs and to specialty process-technology peers. The peer read is 'in line' blended, which is exactly the mispricing the split is designed to correct: standalone, the high-margin STS business should command a premium multiple it cannot earn while buried inside a government-services conglomerate.
forcing_function: The hard, scheduled event is the Mission Technology Solutions spin-off, targeted for the second half of 2026, with the new company's chief executive and chief financial officer already named (June 2026) and carve-out audits underway — a firm, dated corporate event rather than a fixed-price deal. Ahead of that, the second-quarter 2026 earnings report on July 30, 2026 (about three weeks out) and the eventual spin-off Form-10 registration (which reveals each company's capital structure) are the near-term markers that will either confirm the thesis or offer a cleaner entry. Management is also 'open to approaches' on MTS, leaving optionality for an outright sale at a premium.
moderator_conclusion: Where we disagree with the market: the Street's roughly $36 target and roughly 7.5x blended multiple treat KBR as one melting government contractor, but our sum-of-the-parts says the high-margin, technology-led STS crown jewel plus a backlog-rich MTS are worth about $47 in the base case, and the spin-off is the firm, dated mechanism (second half of 2026) to force that re-rating. The risky window over the next few months is real: a second-quarter print on July 30 that could show more MTS revenue runoff and NASA softness, plus the reveal of how much debt loads onto the spin-off — either could flush the stock nearer the adverse $32 case first. Forced-selling pressure has largely already happened — down about 45% on the year, near the 52-week low, with government-linked and index de-risking through the budget-efficiency scare — and insiders are stepping in (four open-market buys and a new roughly $24M stake). Net: the thesis is real and the asymmetry is favorable, but with about 2.9x leverage and a binary earnings event three weeks out, we would let the July 30 print and the spin-off registration clear the decks and buy the wash-out rather than chase here. This is a break-up special situation with a genuine, scheduled catalyst, not a momentum name — a position to size to the spread between today's price and a conservative sum-of-the-parts. On credibility: management delivers on margins, cash and buybacks and has beaten earnings every quarter, but the HomeSafe termination one quarter after reassurances, and the year-long 'awards convert next year' refrain, keep this short of the top score. The moat is narrow but real — proprietary process technology and licensing in STS, incumbency and switching costs on multi-year government programs in MTS — and is holding rather than eroding; the artificial-intelligence and energy-transition forces here look manageable to favorable (STS is an energy-security and sustainable-fuel beneficiary, and government-security barriers protect MTS), not a terminal threat.
